Intro.text: What actually happens during a heart attack, and what should you do?

WhatIsIt.text: Your heart is a muscle that never rests.
It beats about 100,000 times a day, pumping blood around your body.
Like any muscle, it needs its own oxygen supply.
That comes from the coronary arteries, which wrap around the heart.

Blockage.text: Healthy arteries let blood flow freely.
Over years, fat and cholesterol can build up as plaque, narrowing the artery.
If plaque cracks open, a blood clot forms on top of it,
and can block blood flow completely. That is a heart attack.

Damage.text: Without oxygen, the heart muscle below the blockage starts to die.
Damage begins within minutes, and spreads the longer the artery stays blocked.
Fast treatment reopens the artery and saves muscle.

Signs.text: The most common sign is chest pain or pressure that lasts more than a few minutes.
Pain can spread to the arm, jaw, neck or back, often with shortness of breath.
Others feel a cold sweat, nausea, or dizziness.
Women, older people, and people with diabetes may have milder or unusual symptoms.

Act.text: If you suspect a heart attack, call emergency services immediately.
Rest, and chew an aspirin only if the dispatcher or a doctor advises it.
If the person collapses and isn't breathing normally, start CPR, and use an AED if one is nearby.

Prevention.text: Most heart attacks are linked to risks you can change.
Stop smoking, and keep blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar in check.
Stay active, eat well, and see your doctor regularly.

Outro.text: Know the signs. Act fast. You could save a life.
